title: Boneca Ambalabu
observations: The sum splits by bit: bit i adds 2^i times the number of j whose bit i differs from that of a_k.
With cnt_i = how many elements have bit i set, that number is cnt_i when a_k has the bit clear and n - cnt_i when it has it set.
So each k is evaluated in 30 steps after one counting pass; try every k.
nudges: How much does bit 3 alone add to the total, for a fixed k?
If you knew how many elements have bit i set, could you tell how many differ from a_k in that bit?
What can be counted once, before looking at any particular k?

title: Against the Difference
observations: Let dp(i) be the best answer using only the first i elements; it never decreases as i grows.
If a_i is used, it is the last element of a block of a_i copies of the value a_i, so you need the a_i-th most recent position x holding that value, and the candidate is dp(x - 1) + a_i.
Because dp is non-decreasing, taking the latest possible copies is always best, so there is only that one transition besides dp(i - 1). Keep the positions of each value in a list.
nudges: If the last element you keep is a_i, what must the end of your subsequence look like?
Among all ways to choose the earlier copies of that value, why is the most recent set never worse?
What is the smallest summary of a prefix that lets you extend it by one more block?

title: Game with a Fraction
observations: The fraction equals 2/3 exactly when p = 2d and q = 3d, where d = q - p.
Whatever Alice lowers, Bob can lower the other number, so after every pair of moves p and q are both one smaller and d has not changed.

With d fixed and p falling by one each round, p passes through 2d if it starts at or above it. So Bob wins exactly when p < q and p >= 2(q - p); if p >= q Alice only lowers q, and if p < 2(q - p) it is already too late.
nudges: Write q = p + d. What must p and q be, in terms of d, for p/q to equal 2/3?
After Alice lowers one of the numbers, which move by Bob puts q - p back to what it was?
If q - p never changes and p drops by one each round, for which starting values does p ever equal twice that difference?

title: GCD Treasury
observations: After taking g = gcd(a_i, x) from a pile, the pile is still a multiple of g and x is g, so the gcd is g again: a pile you start on can be emptied.
x only ever changes to a divisor of itself, so every pile that is emptied is divisible by the final value of x, which is a divisor of the first x greater than 1.
Conversely, for any prime p dividing x, every pile divisible by p can be emptied in any order. The answer is the largest such sum over the primes dividing x.
nudges: After one theft from pile i, what is the gcd of the new pile and the new x?
Can x ever become something that does not divide the x you started with?
If you decide that x must stay divisible by a prime p throughout, which piles can you empty?

title: Reverse XOR
observations: Write x with exactly y bits (top bit 1). Bit i of the result is x_i xor x_(y-1-i), the same as bit y-1-i: as a y-bit string the result reads the same both ways.
n may be shorter than y bits; the missing leading zeros must mirror trailing zeros, so y is the length of n plus its number of trailing zeros, and n without its trailing zeros must be a palindrome.
If y is odd the middle bit is a bit xor itself, so it must be 0.
These conditions are enough: for a mirrored pair with result 1 use (1, 0), with result 0 use (1, 1).
nudges: Line x up against its reversal, both with the same number of bits. Which two bits of x make bit i of the result, and which make its mirror bit?
The result can have leading zeros even though x cannot. What does the mirror property then say about the low end of n?
What is the middle bit of the result when x has an odd number of bits?

title: Grid Covering
observations: Jumping by a around a ring of n rows reaches every row only if gcd(a, n) = 1, and likewise gcd(b, m) = 1 for columns.

After k full down-right rounds the position is (ka mod n, kb mod m), which repeats every lcm(n, m) rounds. So at most 2 lcm(n, m) tile visits happen, but there are nm = gcd(n, m) lcm(n, m) tiles: gcd(n, m) >= 3 is impossible.

If gcd(n, m) = 1 every pair of remainders occurs. If it is 2, a tile visited in both phases would need a number that is 0 mod n and 1 mod m, impossible when both are even, so the nm visits are nm different tiles.
Answer: yes exactly when gcd(n, a) = 1, gcd(m, b) = 1 and gcd(n, m) <= 2.
nudges: On a ring of n cells, which cells can you reach by repeatedly jumping a cells?
Where are you after k complete rounds of one jump down and one jump right, and after how many rounds does that repeat?
How many tile visits happen before the walk repeats, and how does that compare with the number of tiles?

title: Silhouette
observations: Equal values have equal shadows and a larger value has a strictly larger shadow, so the distinct shadows in sorted order are the running totals of the groups of equal values, starting from 0.

Consecutive distinct shadows differ by (size of the group) x (its value), and the size is how often that shadow occurs in b. So each value except the largest is forced: the difference must divide exactly and the values must increase.
Nothing constrains the largest value, so take the smallest legal one: one more than the value below it (or 1 if there is only one group).
nudges: Two elements have the same shadow. What can you say about their values?
Sort the distinct shadows. What is the difference between two neighbours, in terms of the hidden array?
Which group's value appears in no shadow at all?

title: G-C-D, Unlucky!
observations: Necessary at once: each p_i divides p_(i-1), each s_i divides s_(i+1), and p_n = s_1 because both are the gcd of everything.
Every a_i must be a multiple of both p_i and s_i. If some array works, then a_i = lcm(p_i, s_i) works too: its prefix gcds divide the true ones and are still multiples of p_i.
So build that one smallest candidate and recompute its prefix and suffix gcds; answer yes exactly when they match.
nudges: What must be true of p_(i-1) and p_i in any prefix-gcd array, whatever a is?
Which two given numbers must divide a_i?
If an answer exists and you shrink every a_i to the smallest number allowed by those divisibility conditions, can a prefix gcd change?

title: Alternating Path
observations: Components are independent; add up their answers.
If v is beautiful, every edge at v points away from v, every edge at a neighbour points into it, and so on: the direction at a vertex is fixed by the parity of its distance from v.
A vertex reachable by both an even and an odd walk would need its edges pointing both ways, so a component with an odd cycle gives 0.
In a two-colourable component, making v beautiful makes its whole side beautiful and nothing else, so take the larger side.
nudges: Look only at walks of length one and two from v. What do they force about the edges at v and at its neighbours?
What goes wrong if some vertex can be reached from v in both an even and an odd number of steps?
Once one vertex of a component is beautiful, which other vertices are?

title: Prime Destruction
observations: The numbers never interact, so the answer is a sum over the elements of the cost of reducing one number.
For one number i > k, the first operation picks a prime p dividing i and leaves p independent copies of i/p: cost(i) = min over p of 1 + p * cost(i/p), and cost(i) = 0 for i <= k.
i/p < i, so fill the table upward, with the prime divisors of each number from a sieve.
nudges: Does what you do to one element change what is best for another?
After the first operation on a single number, what sub-problems are you left with, and how many of each?
In what order can the values be solved so that everything needed is already known?

title: XOR Problem
observations: A block has XOR 0 exactly when the prefix XORs at its two ends are equal, so count repeated prefix values instead of blocks.

With x the largest power of two not above n, every prefix XOR is below 2x: only 2x values exist. Appending a prefix value seen 0 times adds 1 to the beauty, seen once adds 0, seen twice or more loses.
So the best beauty is 2x - 1, and the longest array reaching it has every value appear exactly twice: 4x prefix values, length 4x - 1.
Walk the prefix values 0..x-1, back down, then x..2x-1, back down. Neighbouring values in one half XOR to less than x, and the single jump from 0 to x is exactly x, so every element is at most n.
nudges: How can you tell from running XORs alone that a block has XOR 0?
How many different running XOR values are possible at all, and what happens to the beauty the first, second and third time a value shows up?
Rather than choosing the elements, can you choose the sequence of running XORs and read the elements off it?

title: Caveman
observations: An isolated vertex makes it impossible. Otherwise a colouring always exists: colour one edge of each component red-blue and keep giving an uncoloured neighbour the opposite colour.
Swapping the two colours gives another valid colouring, so the count is even and the answer is never 1.
Two components, a path on four vertices (RBRB and RBBR both extend), or a triangle each already give more than two.
What is left is a connected graph with no cycle and no path on four vertices: a star. So the answer is 2 exactly for a star.
nudges: When is there no valid colouring at all, and can you always build one otherwise?
Given one valid colouring, can you name a second without looking at the graph?
Which small pieces inside a graph already force a third colouring, and which connected graphs contain none of them?

title: Median Partition
observations: A block of odd length has median x exactly when (count below x) + (count equal) > (count above) and (count above) + (count equal) > (count below).
Adding these inequalities over all the blocks shows the whole array satisfies them too: the common median can only be the median of the whole array.
With that value fixed, let f(i) be the most blocks the first i elements can be cut into; try every earlier cut j, keeping running counts so that each block is tested in O(1). That is O(n^2).
nudges: How would you decide that a block has median x by counting, without sorting it?
If every block has median y, what do those counts say when you add them up over the whole array?
Once the common value is known, what do you need to remember about a prefix in order to extend it by one more block?

title: Exceptional Segments
observations: With P(i) = 1 xor 2 xor ... xor i, the block (l, r) has XOR 0 exactly when P(l-1) = P(r), and it contains x when l-1 < x <= r.
Computing a few values shows P(i) is i, 1, i+1, 0 as i mod 4 is 0, 1, 2, 3 (provable by induction, four cases).
So the only values that repeat are 0 (at i = 0 and i = 3 mod 4) and 1 (at i = 1 mod 4). Count each kind among 0..x-1 and among x..n by division and multiply.
nudges: Which two running XOR values decide whether the block from l to r has XOR 0?
What are 1 xor 2 xor ... xor i for i = 0 to 8? Do you see a pattern?
Which values of the running XOR can ever occur at two different positions?

title: XOR, Expression and Two Binary Numbers
observations: With A and B the two given numbers and C = A xor B, the XOR of any two of the three is the third, so every number in the sequence is A, B or C.
Which of the three sits at a position depends only on the position mod 3: the midpoint of two positions with different remainders has the third remainder, matching the third value.
So count how many of the positions 1..2^k + 1 fall in each remainder class, and multiply each count by (ones x zeros) of the corresponding number.
nudges: Write out the sequence for k = 3 using letters for the two given numbers. How many different values appear?
Look at the positions where each value appears. What do they have in common?
If p and q have different remainders mod 3 and p + q is even, what is the remainder of their midpoint?

title: XOR Sorting (Easy Version)
observations: A swap of positions whose XOR is not a power of two can be replaced by three swaps through the position that differs only in the highest differing bit, so only powers of two matter and the answer is 0 or a power of two.
With swaps of XOR at most 2^j, an index can never change its bits above bit j: every element stays inside its block of 2^(j+1) consecutive positions.
Inside a block every rearrangement is reachable. So 2^j works exactly when the largest element of each block is at most the smallest of the next; test the O(log n) candidates in O(n) each.
nudges: You want to swap positions i and j whose XOR has several bits set. Can you do it with swaps that each change a single bit of the index?
If only swaps with index XOR at most 2^j are allowed, which positions can a given element ever reach?
Given that every block can be fully sorted but nothing leaves its block, when is the whole array sortable?

title: Chronostasis
observations: Undo the operation: a_i = a_(i-1) + b_i, so a is the running sums of b in some order.
To make a as small as possible position by position, each step should add the smallest unused b that keeps the running sum at least 1, that is the smallest unused value >= 1 - (current sum).
If no unused value is large enough the answer is -1. A sorted multiset with a lower-bound search does each step in O(log n).
nudges: If you knew the order in which the differences were used, how would you rebuild a?
The running sum so far is fixed. Which unused difference makes the next element smallest while still positive?
Why can choosing a larger difference now never rescue a situation that the smallest legal one cannot?

title: Kevin and Puzzle
observations: A liar's left neighbour is honest, so if person i is a liar the true number of liars to their left is a_(i-1) + 1: nothing about a liar's own statement is needed.
Let dp(i) count the arrangements of the first i people in which person i is honest. Person i-1 is either honest (needs a_i = a_(i-1)) or a liar with i-2 honest (needs a_i = a_(i-2) + 1).
The last person is honest or a liar, so the answer is dp(n) + dp(n-1).
nudges: If person i is lying, what do you know for certain about person i-1?
Suppose person i is honest. What are the possibilities for person i-1, and what does each force a_i to be?
Which arrangements does 'person n is honest' leave out, and how are they counted?

title: Kevin and Numbers
observations: Merging is hard to plan forwards, but backwards it is forced: a number x can only have come from floor(x/2) and ceil(x/2).
Work on b: look at its largest number. If a also contains it, cancel both. Otherwise nothing in b can ever produce it except itself, so it must be split.
Exactly n - m splits are available. Keep both multisets in priority queues; fail if a split is needed and none is left, or the largest of a exceeds the largest of b.
nudges: If x was produced by one merge, what were the two numbers?
Run the process backwards from b. What can be done with the largest number present if a does not contain it?
How many backward steps are you allowed in total?

title: Mukhammadali and the Smooth Array
observations: A changed position can be given any value, so the only constraint is on the positions you keep: their values must be non-decreasing from left to right.
Minimising the cost of what you change is the same as maximising the total cost of what you keep.

Let best(i) be the largest kept total of a non-decreasing subsequence ending at i: c_i plus the largest best(j) over j < i with a_j <= a_i. With n up to 8000 the O(n^2) table is enough; the answer is the sum of all c minus the largest best.
nudges: Suppose you have decided which positions stay untouched. When can the rest be filled in to make the array non-decreasing?
Is it easier to describe what you pay for, or what you keep?
What do you need to know about a kept subsequence in order to append one more element to it?

title: Fair and Square
observations: For three vertices in a tree, exactly one vertex c lies on all three connecting paths; every other vertex lies on none or on exactly two of them.
So in the product every value appears to an even power except a_c, which appears cubed: the triple is good exactly when a_c is a perfect square.

Count by c instead of by triple. Remove c; with component sizes s_1..s_k, triples containing c number the sum of s_i s_j, and triples not containing c the sum of s_i s_j s_l, both from one pass keeping running sums. Component sizes come from subtree sizes and n - size.
nudges: Draw three vertices in a tree and the three paths between them. How many times is each vertex of the picture used?
Given that, which single value decides whether the product is a perfect square?
Instead of going through triples, can you fix that special vertex and count the triples it is special for?

title: Minimize Fixed Points
observations: Some positions cannot move: 1, and every prime p with 2p > n, because no other number up to n shares a factor with it.
A cycle in which every number is divisible by one common prime is always good, however long it is.
Group 2..n by largest prime factor and rotate each group. A prime p with 2p <= n is grouped with 2p at least, so the only fixed points are the forced ones.
nudges: Which numbers up to n share no factor with any other number up to n?
If several positions are all multiples of the same prime, in how many ways may you shuffle the values among them?
How can you split 2..n into groups, each sharing a prime, so that as few groups as possible have size one?

title: Elections in Saransk (easy version)
observations: The lcm equals the product exactly when the chosen numbers are pairwise coprime, i.e. every prime divides at most one of them.
Primes do not interact. For one prime, either nobody uses it, or exactly one voter i does, with any exponent from 1 up to its exponent in a_i: that is 1 + (sum of its exponents over all a_i) ways.
Multiply that over every prime that divides some a_i, factorising with a smallest-prime-factor sieve.
nudges: When is the least common multiple of several numbers equal to their product?
Fix one prime. In how many ways can it be handed out among the voters?
Do the choices made for two different primes restrict each other?

title: A Bit Odd
observations: A position with no legal move is a string of equal characters, so try to win in one move: delete all the 1s (plus some 0s) or all the 0s (plus some 1s). That works exactly when some 0 has an odd number of 1s before it, or some 1 has an odd number of 0s after it.
If neither holds, the string is an optional 0, then blocks each equal to 00 or 11, then an optional 1.

In such a string, split any block between the removed part and the rest and both parts get the same character; blocks kept together add an even amount. So the removed part and the remainder have the same inversion parity: after any legal move the remainder is itself a legal move, and the opponent deletes all of it.
So the first player wins exactly when the string is not of that block form.
nudges: What do the positions with no legal move look like, and when can you reach one in a single move?
If no single move wins, what must the string look like, read two characters at a time?
In that case, compare the parity of inversions in the part you delete with the parity in the part you leave. What does that hand your opponent?

title: Array Replacement
observations: Look at the differences d_i = a_(i+1) - a_i. The operation at i swaps d_(i-1) and d_i and changes nothing else.
It is allowed when a_(i-1) and a_(i+1) have the same parity, i.e. when d_(i-1) + d_i is even: the two differences have the same parity.

So a difference can never pass one of the other parity: each maximal run of same-parity differences can be sorted freely, and nothing else is reachable. Sort every run in increasing order and rebuild from a_1.
nudges: What does the operation do to the two gaps on either side of a_i?
What does the parity condition say about those two gaps?
If neighbouring gaps can be swapped only when they have the same parity, which rearrangements of the gaps are possible?

title: Inversion Value of a Permutation
observations: Count the opposite: segments with no inversion. A segment has no inversion exactly when it is increasing, so cut the permutation at every descent into increasing blocks.
If every pair of elements from different blocks is inverted, the inversion-free segments are exactly those inside one block: a block of length L gives L(L-1)/2 of them.

So you need block lengths summing to n with the L(L-1)/2 summing to n(n-1)/2 - k: a small table over (elements used, segments so far). Then fill the first block with the largest numbers in increasing order, the next block with the next largest, and so on.
nudges: Which is easier to describe: a segment that contains an inversion, or one that contains none?
If the permutation is made of increasing runs, how many inversion-free segments does a run of length L contribute?
Given the run lengths, how do you place the numbers so that no segment crossing two runs is increasing?

title: Binary Bubble Sort Inversions
observations: Trying small arrays shows a bubble only moves one element in effect: the first 1 ends up at the very end. A reverse bubble moves the last 0 to the very front.
Moving the first 1 to the end removes one inversion for every 0 after it: (number of 0s) minus (number of leading 0s). The reverse case removes (number of 1s) minus (number of trailing 1s).

Leading 0s and trailing 1s never matter again, so keep two pointers around the active middle part: a bubble drops its first element, a reverse bubble its last, then skip new leading 0s and trailing 1s while updating the counts.
nudges: Run one bubble by hand on 1 1 0 1 0 0. Compare before and after: which elements have effectively moved?
When that one element moves to the end, which inversions disappear?
Which parts of the array can no longer take part in any inversion, and can you stop looking at them?

title: Tea Blend
observations: The number of divisors is the product of (exponent + 1), which is odd exactly when every exponent is even: the number is a perfect square.

Only the parity of each exponent matters, and multiplying numbers XORs their sets of odd-exponent primes. So F(i, j) is a square exactly when a_i and the product of the first j elements have the same set.

Keep a map from the set (hashed) of each prefix to how often it occurs, and add up, over i, the count for the set of a_i. Sets with more than 7 primes can be ignored: no single a_i up to 10^6 has that many.
nudges: Which numbers have an odd number of divisors?
For a product to be a perfect square, what must be true of each prime's exponent in the two factors?
What short summary of a prefix product is enough to tell whether one more factor makes it a square?
